target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is a productive use of already-deceased animals rather than a harmful practice.
objection: School dissection depends on animals that are caught in the wild; wild-capture is inhumane, reduces local populations, and harms biodiversity, so animal dissection is environmentally harmful rather than a harmless use of dead animals.

target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection provides valuable hands-on biology learning and builds fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and critical thinking.
objection: Students can meet the relevant biology learning goals without dissecting real animals, because synthetic models and computer simulations teach as well as or better than dead-animal dissection and are consistent with required standards.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives are sufficient and that simulations can replace real dissection for practical learning.
objection: Fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination are learned through direct physical manipulation and sensorimotor practice, so simulations are unlikely to provide the same practical laboratory training as handling real specimens.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can teach students equally well or better.
objection: Students cannot achieve dissection-level practical laboratory and critical-thinking outcomes equally well with alternatives, because real-animal dissection uniquely provides hands-on specimen handling and associated competencies.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection depends on wild-capture and thus harms biodiversity.
objection: Most classroom dissection specimens are already-deceased meat-industry byproducts, such as fetal pigs destined for landfills, so dissection does not mainly depend on wild-capture that would reduce local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG1’s claim that classroom dissection does not mainly depend on wild-captured animals.
objection: Typical dissection programs do rely mainly on wild-captured specimens rather than already-deceased byproducts, so the claim that dissection is mostly based on dead byproducts is not supported.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection depends on harmful wild-capture.
objection: Animal dissection can rely mainly on already-deceased meat-industry byproducts rather than requiring live wild-capture, so it need not depend on environmentally harmful specimen sourcing.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is unnecessary because AP Biology/NGSS and medical training do not require it, plus alternatives exist.
objection: Animal dissection is not necessary for students to meet required biology learning standards, because the standards do not require it and the methods used to supply specimens are inhumane and environmentally harmful.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection should be rejected because it is unnecessary and harmful.
objection: A teaching method that meaningfully increases students’ interest in science and career aspirations is educationally warranted, so if dissection motivates students toward science careers, that benefit matters educationally.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is environmentally harmful because it uses wild-caught animals.
objection: In common classroom practice, dissection can rely on already-deceased meat-industry byproducts rather than requiring new harm to obtain specimens, so the environmental-harm objection does not fully apply.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection uses already-deceased animals and therefore does not depend on live wild-capture.
objection: Animal dissection depends on inhumane and environmentally harmful wild-capture, which harms local populations and biodiversity, so students should not dissect animals as part of biology education.

target: AG2’s claim that wild-caught animals are obtained alive and therefore dissection depends on live capture.
objection: Wild-caught animals are typically already dead when they are obtained for dissection supply, so typical dissection programs do not mainly involve capturing living animals.

target: AG2’s implication that using fetal pigs and other byproducts creates environmental harm rather than reducing waste.
objection: Repurposing animal byproducts that would otherwise go to landfills reduces landfill waste instead of adding disposal impacts, so dissection using such materials can be environmentally preferable.

target: AG1’s assumption that wild-caught specimens are not already dead when obtained.
objection: Captured wild animals often experience stress, injury, and transport conditions that increase the likelihood they die before delivery, so the assumption that wild-caught specimens are not already dead when obtained is not warranted.

target: AG1’s broader claim that students should dissect animals because dissection is educationally worthwhile despite harms.
objection: Because dissection depends on inhumane treatment and environmental harm, and because schools have an educational responsibility to avoid requiring harmful activities when non-harmful alternatives exist, students should not be required to dissect animals.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is not justified because alternatives can also motivate students.
objection: If a teaching method meaningfully increases students’ interest in science and career aspirations, then using it in biology instruction is educationally warranted, even if it is not the only way to teach content.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives match dissection’s motivational benefits.
objection: Schools are justified in including, and when appropriate requiring, animal dissection because alternatives have not been shown to produce equally strong “aha moments” and career-motivation effects.

target: AG1’s claim that only real-animal dissection can produce the “aha moments” and motivation that matter educationally.
objection: If a teaching method provides active, realistic exploration of biological structures, it can generate “aha moments” and comparable science/career motivation, and high-quality synthetic models and simulations can do that.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives have not been shown to match dissection’s motivational benefits.
objection: Non-dissection alternatives can generate “aha moments” and comparable science/career-motivation effects, so the claim that alternatives have not been shown to match dissection’s motivational benefits is undermined.
